extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of constitutional design and political theory (lawmakers, political philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and rules for designing/evaluating a 'right constitution of a commonwealth', especially comparing simple democracies and mixed (three-branch) governments; addresses offices, suffrages, militia, education, judiciary, and factional control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit duration of great powers and commands
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not permit great powers and commands to continue long, and limit them in point of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and historical examples: Roman laws limiting terms (e.g., censor, dictatorial offices), Livy and Cicero's complaints about holding high office beyond fixed months; continuance in high office constantly exposed the state to being overturned and converted into absolute monarchy. In mixed constitutions such limits may be less necessary but still useful; in simple democracies they are often set aside by popular majorities. Anti-pattern: allowing generals/administrators to keep command indefinitely (leads to empire/despotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit concentration of high offices within one family
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to let two of one family bear offices of high trust at one time, nor to permit a continuation of great powers in anyone family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original Roman rules: 'Ne duo vel plures ex una familia magnos magistratus gerant eodem tempore' and 'Ne magna imperia ab una familia prescribantur.' Rationale: in aristocracies these rules guard against powerful families dominating the state; examples/cautions: Medici, House of Orange, papal families. Practical note: rule is often impracticable in simple democracies where the people will set it aside for favourites; in a properly mixed constitution it can be more readily observed and enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the majesty and purity of suffrages (votes)
rubrics_metrics.description: To hold up the majesty and authority of their suffrages or votes entire, untainted with the influence or mixture of any commanding power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: preserve independence and integrity of assemblies (senates or people) from corruption, flattery, artifice, bribes, or fear. Historical illustrations: when Rome's suffrages were corrupted or controlled (e.g., by Sylla, Caesar), liberty was lost in effect even if forms remained. Anti-pattern: treating popular suffrage as absolute and uncontroulled, which can enable demagogues and factional domination; likewise, allowing other powers to influence or pay for votes undermines liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train the people and lodge the militia in the people's hands
rubrics_metrics.description: That the people be continually trained up in the exercise of arms, and the militia lodged only in the people's hands (or that part most firm to the interest of liberty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support from Aristotle and ancient practice: Rome and Greek states trained citizens as militia; the sword and sovereignty go together. Intended benefit: militia in citizens' hands ties military power to the people who hold sovereignty. Caveat/antipattern: when the people become sovereign without effective checks, keeping arms broadly may enable factional violence, standing armies raised by popular majorities, or civil war. The page notes the clause limiting militia to 'that part most firm to the interest of liberty' was a practical insertion to allow disarming suspected enemies (e.g., royalists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure militia is created, directed, and commanded by law under executive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental law of the militia is that it be created, directed, and commanded by the laws, and ever for the support of the laws; the militia should obey the executive power which represents the whole people in the execution of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-argument to citizen militia absolutism: to prevent dissolution of government and civil war, the militia must be organized under legal authority and the executive (not left to individual discretion). Historical reasoning: when sovereignty shifts to an uncontrolled majority, standing armies and praetorian bands supplanted militias (e.g., Caesar), leading to despotism. Practical rule: place military command within constitutional legal structures to avoid both private militias and unaccountable popular control of arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate children in the principles of the constituted government
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should be educated and instructed in the principles of freedom; the institution of youth should be accommodated to that form of government under which they live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: impressions formed in youth persist into adulthood; public education is particularly indispensable under a free government to produce citizens fit for public service. Historical examples: difficulty Rome faced establishing aristocracy because youth had been educated under monarchy; in mixed governments education is widespread because many may be called to public service. Practical concern: in simple democracies public education may be underprovided (expense), leaving education to private munificence and producing inequality of civic knowledge—an anti-pattern undermining the stability of a republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use liberty with moderation to prevent licentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To use liberty with moderation, lest it turn to licentiousness; licentiousness, being a tyranny itself, usually occasions corruption and conversion of a free state into monarchical tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admonition to citizens: moderation alone (lectures, sermons) is insufficient; the energy of laws must back moral exhortations. Risks identified: elections and patronage can protect licentious elites; public money and office distribution can foster debauchery and corruption. In a mixed government the law and magistracy can reinforce moderation; in a simple democracy these legal enforcements are weaker or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid civil dissensions and refrain from using extreme remedies for ordinary faults
rubrics_metrics.description: It is above all things necessary to avoid civil dissensions, and the uttermost remedy is not to be used upon every distemper or default of those that shall be intrusted with the people's power and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim: minimize factional conflict and avoid recourse to violence (civil war) as an ordinary political remedy. The page argues that in simple democracies there is often no peaceful remedy for the minority except tumult or arms; therefore a constitution should provide means to compose disputes. Anti-pattern: allowing every political grievance to be answered by the 'uttermost remedy' (violence), which multiplies disorders and destabilizes the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an upright, independent judiciary to decide controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: An upright independent tribunal to judge of controversies is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: an independent judiciary resolves disputes between classes (rich/poor, higher/lower) without yielding to the majority's immediate will. In mixed governments judges are secured because removal requires concurrence of branches; in simple democracies judges are dependent (commissions durante bene placito) and therefore at the mercy of the majority. Essential features: formal trials, full defence, fixed tenure sufficient to prevent arbitrary removal. Anti-pattern: judges removable at majority whim and courts used as tools of the ruling majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitute effectual controls in the constitution to check popular neglect and majority abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a people may lose their liberty by neglect or fault, constitutions must provide effectual control — checks and balances — to prevent the concentration and abuse of power even if the people are negligent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: it is humiliating and destructive to tell citizens they lost liberty solely by general neglect; therefore constitutions should build safeguards (e.g., multiple branches, limits on office duration, protections for suffrages) so that predictable popular faults do not destroy liberty. Examples: the value of a senate or mixed constitution to check the people's excesses; anti-pattern: leaving all power to single assemblies without institutional counterweights, which enables Sylla/Caesar-style usurpations.
